extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially speculative fiction) seeking guidance on story structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting and applying narrative structures (three-act, seven-point, kishōtenketsu, etc.) to enhance elements like character, plot, tension, worldbuilding, or twist. Emphasizes intentional use of microstructures within larger frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intentional with structure
rubrics_metrics.description: We should be a lot more intentional with structure as we write; structure at this level of detail gets overlooked a lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t treat structure as something that ‘just happens’—deliberately choose structural techniques to serve the story. Look beyond high-level frameworks and pay attention to microstructures that define how narrative elements unfold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose structure to highlight the story's most important aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself, what is the most important aspect of your story that you’re trying to explore? Is it the character, the relationships, the worldbuilding, or a twist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match structure to emphasis: character/relationships → multiple timelines or multiple perspectives; worldbuilding → structures built around setting (e.g., maps, footnotes); twist-driven stories → structures that support staged reveals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two approaches: story-first vs structure-first
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers start with a story/character and then find a structure to fit; others start with a structure or structural element and then develop characters and plot around it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which approach you’re using; each has different challenges. If story is fixed, choose a structure that enhances the established elements; if structure is fixed, use it as the organizing principle for developing characters and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blindly copying the masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying the masters (e.g., rote adoption of Save the Cat) can produce repeatable but ultimately similar stories: 'what you used to do as an artist… you would take a painting and make an exact copy…' This reflex leads to repeating the same kind of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use master-structures as learning tools (trace compositional circles, borrow shapes) but intentionally replace elements to avoid derivative repetition. Be aware of the anti-pattern of relying on a single familiar structure for every story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-Western and alternative structures (kishōtenketsu etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many options besides Western three-act norms; for example kishōtenketsu is a four-act structure (ki: introduction, sho: development, ten: twist, tetsu: conclusion) that can be very satisfying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study alternative cultural forms (kishōtenketsu, rule-of-five/nine variants) and consider how they might better serve certain stories, especially those that don’t fit conventional Western expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure sets audience expectations; manage deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When people recognize the beginning of a structure, they set expectations for that structure to unfold per formula; if the work doesn't follow it, some audience members may be disappointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you plan to deviate from a familiar structure, either manage reader expectations or 'educate' the audience through other cues so the deviation feels intentional rather than mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map story beats to known frameworks where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you’ve identified beats in character transformation, geography, or plot, ask: does this map onto an existing structure I know how to use (seven points, kishōtenketsu, Freytag, etc.)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a step back to see whether your emergent beat-map aligns with a known structure you can employ; this reduces slop and helps you shape pacing and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microstructures and techniques within overarching frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond Freytag’s Triangle, Save the Cat, and Truby’s steps, there are specific techniques (microstructures) that fit into larger narrative shapes and are often overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and apply smaller structural techniques (scene-level beats, perspective shifts, timeline fragments, footnotes, maps) to refine how the larger framework operates in your story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let setting and 'geometry' influence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the setting or the geography of a world suggests the structure (e.g., Avatar: three seasons focusing on Water, Earth, Fire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elements like geography, institutional divisions, or other worldbuilding features as natural structural divisions to explore different facets of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose structure to control pacing and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure you choose will change the pacing and the tension of the story and can help draw out elements like worldbuilding, character growth, or surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about how structural choices (act breaks, multiple timelines, point-of-view changes) affect reader momentum and the buildup/release of tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structure to stage transformation and landmark beats
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character undergoes transformation, the beats in that transformation become structural landmarks around which the story paces itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify transformation beats early and build structure around those landmarks so the reader experiences change clearly and rhythmically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with structure to broaden story possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: There are lots of different structures; choosing different ones will broaden the kinds of stories you can tell and avoid repeating the same results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try unfamiliar structures and hybrid approaches to discover new narrative effects; be open to structures that emphasize different story dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by analyzing examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: pick a favorite book with an interesting structure and identify how the author’s chosen structure enhances tension, plot, or character development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice structural analysis on existing works (e.g., The Inheritance of Orquídea Divina, Encanto, Parasite) to see concrete ways structures function and to inspire application in your own writing.
